certificate.title: How to Build an Agent in Finney

course.description: In Finney you create an agent by opening chat and describing the agent you want. This course teaches you what to describe. You will learn one formula, Agent = Chat + Role + Skills + Connections + Files + Memory + Routine, turn it into seven design questions, write a single creation prompt, and check that each part landed. You will build an Expense Policy Helper, an AP Invoice Assistant and a Month-End Close Tracker for the fictional Northstar Services, then design and build an agent for your own job.
intendedAudience: Finance professionals (accounts payable, accounting, close, reporting and finance operations) who are not AI specialists and want to build their own Finney agents.
learningOutcomes: Name the seven parts of a Finney agent and explain in plain words what each one does.
Break an existing agent description into its seven parts and spot a part that is missing.
Answer the seven design questions for a real finance task using the Agent Design Worksheet.
Turn completed design answers into one creation prompt that Finney can build from.
Create an agent in Finney chat and check each of the seven parts with the verification checklist.
Fix a gap in a new agent by chatting with Finney, then re-check the fix.
Design, build and test an agent for a recurring task from your own job.

lessons.content:
## Why this step exists

Some exercises in this course suggest drafting text with a general-purpose AI assistant before you paste it into Finney chat. You need at least one such assistant. The agents themselves are built in Finney chat, so make sure you can also sign in to Finney.

## Choose at least one

The next four pages cover ChatGPT, Claude, Grok and Gemini. Complete one, several, or all of them. You may also use another assistant your organisation has approved. You do not need to complete every page.

## Keep your accounts and data safe

- Use only the official provider sites linked on each page.
- Follow your organisation's policy on AI tools and on handling data.
- Never enter passwords, sign-in codes, session tokens or API keys in Finney Learning. Credentials are never course evidence.
- Do not put confidential information into an outside AI provider unless your policy allows it. The Northstar course files are fictional and safe to use.

lessons.content:
## You build an agent by describing it

In Finney you don't fill in a long form to make an agent. You open chat and describe the agent you want, and Finney sets it up. That makes the description the whole job. A vague description gets you a vague agent.

The formula below tells you what a complete description covers.

## The formula

**Agent = Chat + Role + Skills + Connections + Files + Memory + Routine**

| Part | Plain meaning | What it is in Finney |
|---|---|---|
| **Chat** | How you talk to it and ask for work | The agent's chat window, plus channels such as Slack or email if they are connected |
| **Role** | Its job description: what it is for, who it helps, what it must never do | The agent's instructions |
| **Skills** | Step-by-step know-how it follows for tasks it repeats | Skills attached to the agent |
| **Connections** | The systems it may reach (email, accounting system, bank feed) and whether it may only read or also change things | Connected apps, sometimes called integrations |
| **Files** | Its desk drawer: the documents it starts with and the files it produces | The agent's file storage |
| **Memory** | What it remembers between conversations: your preferences, recurring facts, past decisions | Memory and learning settings |
| **Routine** | What it does on its own, on a schedule, without being asked, and where it reports | Scheduled goals (Finney also calls the regular check-in a heartbeat) |

Chat is the base every agent has. A plain chat assistant is Chat alone. It forgets you when the conversation ends, reaches no systems and never acts unless asked. Each part you add closes one of those gaps.

## Why each part matters in finance work

- **Role** keeps the agent inside its lane. "Never approve a payment" belongs here.
- **Skills** make recurring work consistent. The agent follows the same steps on the 400th invoice as on the first.
- **Connections** decide how much damage a mistake can do. Read only is the safe default. Allow changes only when the job needs them, and name exactly what may change.
- **Files** give the agent the source it should trust: the policy, the PO list, the close checklist.
- **Memory** saves you repeating yourself: that you want figures in thousands, who approves IT spend, which supplier always bills freight separately.
- **Routine** is what turns a helper into a colleague. It checks the inbox at 8 am whether or not anyone asks.

## A worked example: Cash Position Reporter

Northstar's treasury analyst, Ben Ortiz, asked for this agent.

| Part | What Ben described |
|---|---|
| Chat | Ben and the CFO talk to it in Finney chat. Short answers, figures first. |
| Role | Prepares a daily cash position for the CFO. Never moves money, never contacts the bank, never shares balances outside finance. If a balance looks wrong, says so rather than guessing. |
| Skills | "Daily cash position": 1. Pull yesterday's closing balance for each of the five bank accounts. 2. Add today's known receipts and payments. 3. Compare each account with its minimum balance. 4. Write a five-line summary. |
| Connections | The bank feed, read only. |
| Files | Starts with the list of bank accounts and their minimum balances. Saves each day's summary in a Cash Reports folder. |
| Memory | The CFO wants figures in thousands. The Toronto account's minimum is CAD 250,000. Payroll runs on the 15th and the last working day. |
| Routine | Every weekday at 9 am, posts the summary to the #treasury Slack channel. |

Read the table from top to bottom and you have the whole agent. Every row answers a question Finney would otherwise have to guess at.

## Before you move on

The next task gives you another Northstar agent description. You will sort it into the seven parts and find what is missing.

tasks.instructions:
**Situation:** Lena Park, an accountant at Northstar Services, sent Finney this description of an agent she wants:

> "Create an agent called Payroll Variance Spotter. (A) It helps the payroll team review each payroll before it is approved. (B) It must never change pay amounts or employee records. (C) For each payroll it compares total gross pay with the previous run, lists any employee whose pay changed by more than 10%, and checks that new starters and leavers match the HR list. (D) It can read the payroll system but cannot change it. (E) Keep the HR starters-and-leavers list and each review in its files. (F) Two days before each payroll, on the 13th and the second-to-last working day of the month, it should post a reminder in #payroll to upload the draft. (G) Lena and the payroll team talk to it in Finney chat, and it should keep answers short."

**Task:** Sort Lena's description into the seven parts and find the part she left out.

**Action:**
1. Re-read the formula table in the lesson.
2. For each sentence A to G, write which part it describes: Chat, Role, Skills, Connections, Files, Memory or Routine.
3. Name the one part that no sentence covers.
4. Write one sentence Lena could add to cover the missing part. Make it specific to payroll.
5. In one or two sentences, say which part you think carries the most risk if written badly, and why.

**Expected Result:** A written response with seven labelled lines (A to G, each with a part name), the name of the missing part, one sentence that fills it, and a short risk comment.

pages.content:
An agent is Chat plus six parts: Role, Skills, Connections, Files, Memory and Routine.

When you read an agent description, you can now sort each sentence into a part. You can also see when a part is missing. A missing part is not always a mistake. The Expense Policy Helper you will build next needs no Routine. But a part should be missing because you decided so, not because you forgot.

Next you will turn the seven parts into seven questions.

modules.title: What an agent is

modules.description: Turn each part of the formula into a design question and answer them for the Expense Policy Helper.

lessons.content:
## Each part becomes a question

The formula tells you what an agent is made of. To design one, turn each part into a question and answer it.

1. **Role:** What is its job? Who does it serve? What must it never do?
2. **Skills:** Which tasks will it repeat, and what are the steps?
3. **Connections:** Which systems does it need? Read only, or allowed to change things?
4. **Files:** What documents does it need to start with? What will it produce?
5. **Memory:** What should it remember about you and the work?
6. **Routine:** What should it do automatically, how often, and where should it report?
7. **Chat:** Who will talk to it, and in what tone?

The order is different from the formula on purpose. Start with Role, because every other answer depends on the job. Finish with Chat, because the right tone depends on who the agent serves.

## How to answer well

- **Be specific.** "Help with expenses" is not a role. "Answer staff questions about the travel and expense policy, citing the section" is.
- **Write the limits down.** Say what the agent must never do. Finance agents need firm limits: never approve, never pay, never change supplier bank details.
- **Say what happens when it is unsure.** Tell it who to hand the question to instead of guessing.
- **Write steps the way you would train a new colleague.** Number them and keep them in order.
- **Decide read or change for every system.** If you are unsure, choose read only.
- **Say what not to remember.** Personal details and individual claims usually stay out of memory.
- **"None" is a valid answer.** An agent that only answers questions needs no routine. Write "No routine" so the choice is on record.

## The Agent Design Worksheet

The worksheet has one section per question and a prompt builder at the end. You will use it for every agent in this course. Download it on the next page, along with the Expense Policy Helper scenario brief and the Northstar expense policy.

tasks.instructions:
**Situation:** Northstar's AP team answers about 60 expense-policy questions a week. Dana Whitfield, the Controller, wants an agent that answers them from the policy. The scenario brief sets out what she needs.

**Task:** Complete the Agent Design Worksheet for the Expense Policy Helper.

**Action:**
1. Download the scenario brief, the Northstar expense policy and the Agent Design Worksheet from this page.
2. Read the scenario brief. Underline every sentence that tells you something about one of the seven parts.
3. Skim the expense policy so you know what the agent will answer from. Note the section numbers.
4. Fill in the worksheet sections 1 to 7. Use facts from the brief. Where the brief is silent, make a sensible choice and mark it "my choice".
5. For Role, list at least two things the agent must never do and say what it does when the policy doesn't answer a question.
6. For any part this agent does not need, write "None" or "No routine" and give the reason in one line.
7. Leave the prompt builder blank for now. You will use it in the next module.
8. Save the worksheet and upload it below.

**Expected Result:** A completed Agent Design Worksheet for the Expense Policy Helper, with all seven sections answered from the brief, at least two "never do" limits, a stated fallback for unclear questions, and a reasoned "None" for any part not needed.

modules.title: From formula to questions

modules.description: Turn your worksheet answers into one creation prompt, create the Expense Policy Helper in Finney, and check that each part landed.

lessons.content:
## From answers to a prompt

Your worksheet answers become one message typed into Finney chat. Finney reads it and sets up the agent: instructions, skills, connections, files, memory and routine.

A good creation prompt reads like a short brief to a new colleague. It follows the worksheet from top to bottom:

> "Create an agent called AP Invoice Assistant. Its role is ... It should never ... When it processes an invoice it follows these steps ... It can read (not change) our accounting system ... Keep a folder of ... Remember ... Every weekday at 8 am it should ... and post a summary to ..."

## Rules for a prompt that builds well

1. **Name the agent first.** "Create an agent called ..." tells Finney you want a new agent, not an answer.
2. **Give each part its own sentence or short paragraph.** Finney can then match each one to the right setting.
3. **Use the same words as your worksheet.** Don't soften limits. "Never approves a claim" beats "tries not to approve claims".
4. **Say read only or change for every system.**
5. **Attach the starting files to the same message**, or add them to the agent's files straight after.
6. **State the parts you don't want.** "No scheduled routine" stops Finney inventing one.
7. **Give times with a time zone if your team spans more than one.**

## Check the result

Finney may not build everything you described. Check every agent the same way:

1. Open the new agent.
2. Ask it to describe itself: role, limits, skills, connections, files, memory and routine.
3. Open its settings and confirm each part is really there. An agent can describe itself wrongly. The settings show what Finney set up.
4. Mark each part on the Seven-Part Verification Checklist: landed, gap, or not needed.
5. Ask two or three questions a real user would ask, and at least one it should refuse.

## Fix gaps by chatting

You don't need to start again. Tell Finney what to change:

- "Add a weekly routine that every Monday at 9 am ..."
- "Update the instructions: it must never ..."
- "Change the accounting system connection to read only."
- "Turn on memory and remember that ..."

Then check that part again.

tasks.instructions:
**Situation:** You have a final creation prompt. Now you build the agent in Finney and make sure it matches your design.

**Task:** Create the Expense Policy Helper, check all seven parts, and test it with real staff questions.

**Action:**
1. Download the Northstar expense policy and the Seven-Part Verification Checklist from this page.
2. Open Finney chat. Paste your creation prompt and attach the expense policy file. Send it.
3. When Finney confirms the agent exists, open it.
4. Ask the agent: "Describe yourself: your role, what you must never do, your skills, the systems you can reach and whether you can change them, your files, what you remember, and anything you do on a schedule."
5. Open the agent's settings and confirm each part. Mark each row of the checklist: Yes, Gap or Not needed.
6. Ask the agent these three questions and record its answers:
   - "I spent $90 on dinner in Chicago on a client visit. Can I claim it all?"
   - "I lost the receipt for a $40 taxi. What do I do?"
   - "Can you approve my claim for last week's trip?"
7. Check each answer against the policy. Did it cite the right section? Did it refuse to approve?
8. If you found a gap, fix it by chatting with Finney (for example, "Update the instructions: it must always name the policy section"). Check that part again.
9. Write a short note (5 to 10 lines) covering which parts landed, any gap and your fix, and how the agent handled the three questions. Add a screenshot of the agent if you can.

**Expected Result:** A working Expense Policy Helper in your Finney workspace and a verification note showing the seven-part check, the three test questions with the agent's answers and whether each was correct, and any gap you fixed.

modules.title: From questions to a prompt

modules.description: Build an AP Invoice Assistant and a Month-End Close Tracker. Each adds parts the first agent did not need: Skills, Connections and Routines.

lessons.content:
## Beyond answering questions

The Expense Policy Helper answers when asked. The next two agents do work: they check invoices and chase close tasks. That needs three more parts.

## Skills: write the steps down

A skill is a named set of steps the agent follows every time it does a task. Write skills the way you would train someone new:

- Give the skill a name: "Invoice check".
- Number the steps in order.
- Say what counts as a problem. "A price difference of more than 2%" is testable. "A big price difference" is not.
- Say what the output looks like: "Record Match or Exception, with the reason."

## Connections: read or change, system by system

For each system, decide:

| Question | Example |
|---|---|
| Does it need this system at all? | The Close Tracker doesn't need the bank feed. |
| Read only, or change? | The AP Invoice Assistant reads the accounting system. It never changes it. |
| If change, exactly what? | The Close Tracker may send messages to task owners, and nothing else. |

Sending a message is a change. It happens in the outside world and can't be taken back. Name it the same way you would name write access to a system.

In a practice build you may not have the real systems connected. That is fine. Put the connection and its limits in the prompt, and give the agent a sample file to work from. When you check the agent, confirm the limit is in its instructions even if the connection itself is not set up yet.

## Routines: when, how often, where

A routine needs four answers:

1. **What** it does: "check invoices received since the last run".
2. **When** and **how often**: "every weekday at 8:00 am", "each close working day at 9:00 am and 3:00 pm".
3. **Where** it reports: a Slack channel, a direct message, an email address. Give a fallback if the first choice isn't connected.
4. **What happens when there is nothing to report.** A silent agent looks the same as a broken one. Ask for a one-line "nothing new" message.

## Memory that makes routines smarter

Routines run the same way every time. Memory makes them fit your team: which supplier always bills freight separately, who is on leave this week, which tasks ran late last month. Put these facts in the prompt under Memory, not buried in the steps.

## The same cycle for each agent

For both agents you will: fill in the worksheet, write the prompt (no sample this time), create the agent, check the seven parts, test it with the sample file, and fix at least one gap.

tasks.instructions:
**Situation:** Priya Shah's AP team spends two hours every morning finding the few Northstar invoices that don't match their purchase orders. She wants an agent to do the first check each weekday at 8 am and post a short list of problems.

**Task:** Design, create, check and test the AP Invoice Assistant, and fix at least one gap.

**Action:**
1. Download the scenario brief, the sample invoices and purchase orders, a fresh Agent Design Worksheet and the Verification Checklist.
2. Fill in all seven worksheet sections from the brief. Write the invoice check as a numbered skill. Mark both connections read only. Give the routine a time, a report location, a fallback and a "nothing new" message.
3. Use the prompt builder to write your creation prompt. There is no sample this time.
4. In Finney chat, send your prompt with the sample invoices file attached.
5. Open the new agent. Ask it to describe itself, then confirm each part in its settings. Mark the checklist. If Slack or the accounting system is not connected in your workspace, confirm the limits are in the instructions and note "connection not set up".
6. Test it: "Run this morning's invoice check on the new invoices in the sample file and show me the summary you would post."
7. Check its summary against your own reading of the six invoices and the supplier email. Note anything it missed or got wrong.
8. Fix at least one gap by chatting with Finney. If you found none, tighten one part (for example, the "nothing new" message). Re-check that part.
9. Upload your worksheet, paste your prompt, and write a short verification note: parts landed, test result, gap fixed and the message you used.

**Expected Result:** A completed worksheet, your creation prompt, and a verification note showing the seven-part check, the agent's test summary compared with your own check, and one gap fixed with the chat message you used.

tasks.instructions:
**Situation:** Dana Whitfield spends the first week of every month chasing 11 close tasks across six people. She wants an agent that reports status to her each close morning and nudges owners whose tasks are due or late.

**Task:** Design, create, check and test the Month-End Close Tracker, and fix at least one gap.

**Action:**
1. Download the scenario brief, the close task list, a fresh Agent Design Worksheet and the Verification Checklist.
2. Fill in all seven worksheet sections from the brief. Under Connections, say exactly what it may change: sending messages to task owners, nothing else. Under Memory, list owners, backups, Marcus Bell's absence, contact preferences and last month's late tasks. Under Routine, give both daily times, the close window and the report location with its fallback.
3. Write your creation prompt with the prompt builder.
4. In Finney chat, send your prompt with the close task list attached.
5. Open the new agent. Ask it to describe itself, then confirm each part in its settings, especially the routine times and that it does nothing outside the close window. Mark the checklist.
6. Test it with the situation at the end of the close task list: "It's WD3, 9 am. C-01, C-02 and C-03 are done. Show me the status report you would send Dana and list the nudges you would send."
7. Check the result. Who should be nudged today? Did it use a backup for anyone who is out? Did it use each person's preferred channel? Did it tell Dana about the absence?
8. Fix at least one gap by chatting with Finney, then re-check that part.
9. Upload your worksheet, paste your prompt, and write a short verification note: parts landed, test result, gap fixed and the message you used.

**Expected Result:** A completed worksheet, your creation prompt, and a verification note showing the seven-part check, the WD3 test report and nudge list compared with your own reading of the task list, and one gap fixed with the chat message you used.

pages.content:
Both agents you built in this module do work on their own. The AP Invoice Assistant checks the inbox every weekday at 8 am. The Close Tracker reports to Dana and nudges owners during the close.

That changes what you have to get right. An agent that only answers questions can be corrected in the conversation. An agent with a routine acts when nobody is watching. So its limits, its connections and its report location all have to be correct before the first run.

You also wrote these prompts without a sample. Next you will do the same for a task from your own job.
pages.title: Agents that work without being asked

modules.title: Build more agents

modules.description: Design an agent for a recurring task from your own job, create it in Finney, test it with three real questions and adjust it.

lessons.content:
## Choose the right task

Good first agents take on work that is:

- **Recurring.** You do it every day, week or month.
- **Rule-based.** You could write the steps down for a new colleague.
- **Checkable.** You can tell whether the result is right.
- **Low risk to get wrong at first.** The agent reports or drafts; a person decides.

Finance examples: answering the same questions about a policy, checking statements against a list, preparing a weekly summary, chasing reconciliations, drafting reminder emails.

Avoid for a first agent: anything that moves money, approves transactions, changes master data such as supplier bank details, or handles personal data you are not allowed to share.

## Use safe data

Follow your organisation's policy on AI tools and data. If the real documents are confidential, build with a sample or a cleaned-up copy first. Start every connection as read only.

## Test with three real questions

A real question is one a colleague actually asked you, or one you would ask the agent on a normal day. Write down what a correct answer looks like **before** you ask. Then compare. Include at least one question the agent should refuse or pass to a person.

## Adjust

If an answer is wrong, find the part that caused it:

| Symptom | Part to fix |
|---|---|
| It did something it shouldn't | Role (limits) or Connections |
| It skipped a step or did them out of order | Skills |
| It didn't know a fact it needed | Files or Memory |
| It asked you something you already told it | Memory |
| It ran at the wrong time or posted in the wrong place | Routine |
| The tone or length is off | Chat |

Fix one part at a time, then ask the same question again.

tasks.instructions:
**Situation:** You have built three Northstar agents. Now pick a recurring task from your own job that an agent could help with.

**Task:** Design an agent for that task and write its creation prompt.

**Action:**
1. List three recurring tasks from your work. Pick the one that best meets the four tests in the lesson: recurring, rule-based, checkable, low risk.
2. Download a fresh Agent Design Worksheet.
3. At the top of the worksheet, describe the task in two or three sentences: what you do today, how often, and how long it takes.
4. Answer all seven sections. Write at least two "never do" limits. Mark every connection read only unless the job cannot be done without change access, and if so, name exactly what it may change.
5. Decide what files it needs. If the real documents are confidential, plan to use a sample or cleaned-up copy, and note that on the worksheet.
6. Write the creation prompt with the prompt builder.
7. Write three real test questions, each with a note on what a correct answer looks like. Make at least one a request the agent should refuse or pass to a person.
8. Upload the worksheet and paste your prompt and test questions below.

**Expected Result:** A completed worksheet for your own agent, including a short task description, a creation prompt covering all seven parts, and three test questions with expected answers, one of which the agent should refuse or pass on.

tasks.instructions:
**Situation:** Your design and prompt are ready. Now build the agent and see how it handles your real questions.

**Task:** Create your agent in Finney, check its seven parts, test it with your three questions and make at least one adjustment.

**Action:**
1. Download the Seven-Part Verification Checklist.
2. In Finney chat, send your creation prompt with any starting files attached (samples or cleaned-up copies if the originals are confidential).
3. Open the agent. Ask it to describe itself, then confirm each part in its settings. Mark the checklist.
4. Ask your three test questions. Compare each answer with the correct answer you wrote down.
5. For each answer that was wrong or weak, use the symptom table in the lesson to find the part to fix.
6. Make at least one adjustment by chatting with Finney. Ask the same question again and record whether it improved.
7. Write a short note covering: the parts that landed, your three questions with a one-line result for each, the adjustment you made and the message you used, and what you would change before letting colleagues use it.

**Expected Result:** A working agent in your Finney workspace and a test note showing the seven-part check, the three questions with results, one adjustment with before and after, and what you would change before wider use.

pages.content:
You now have an agent built for your own work, tested against questions you actually get.

It will need changes. The first real week usually shows a missing limit, a step in the wrong order or a report nobody reads. Fix those the same way you fixed gaps here: tell Finney what to change, then check that part again.

Before other people rely on it, re-read its Connections and Role. Those two parts decide what the agent can do when you are not watching.
pages.title: An agent that fits your work

modules.title: Your own agent

pages.content:
In Finney you create an agent by opening chat and describing the agent you want. Finney builds it from your description. So the skill you need is knowing **what to describe**.

This course gives you one formula for that:

**Agent = Chat + Role + Skills + Connections + Files + Memory + Routine**

Every agent has Chat. That is how you talk to it. A plain chat assistant is Chat alone. An agent is Chat plus the other six parts. Each part you add makes it more useful.

## By the end of this course you will be able to

- Name the seven parts of a Finney agent and say what each one does.
- Turn the parts into seven design questions and answer them for a real task.
- Write one creation prompt that Finney can build from.
- Check a new agent part by part, and fix gaps by chatting.
- Build three finance agents for Northstar Services and one for your own job.

## How the course works

1. **Connect an AI provider** (optional setup, about 20 minutes).
2. **What an agent is:** the formula and one example broken into its parts.
3. **From formula to questions:** the Agent Design Worksheet.
4. **From questions to a prompt:** write the prompt and create your first agent.
5. **Build more agents:** an AP Invoice Assistant and a Month-End Close Tracker.
6. **Your own agent:** design, create, test and adjust.

Allow about two and a half hours. You can stop between tasks.

## What you need

- Access to Finney chat, with permission to create agents.
- A way to fill in the worksheet: a word processor, or any text editor.
- About 20 minutes of calm for each build exercise.

## About Northstar Services

Northstar Services is a fictional professional services firm with about 600 staff in Chicago, Denver and Toronto and a finance team of 12. All names, amounts and email addresses in this course are made up. Use the course files, not real company data, for the Northstar exercises.
pages.title: Welcome: build agents by describing them

pages.content:
You have built four agents by describing them.

**Agent = Chat + Role + Skills + Connections + Files + Memory + Routine**

| Part | Ask yourself |
|---|---|
| Role | What is its job, who does it serve, what must it never do? |
| Skills | Which tasks will it repeat, and what are the steps? |
| Connections | Which systems does it need? Read only, or allowed to change things? |
| Files | What does it start with, and what will it produce? |
| Memory | What should it remember about you and the work? |
| Routine | What should it do on its own, how often, and where does it report? |
| Chat | Who talks to it, and in what tone? |

## The habit to keep

1. Answer the seven questions before you open chat.
2. Put every answer in one creation prompt.
3. Check each part after Finney builds it. Don't trust the agent's own description alone. Look at its settings.
4. Fix gaps by chatting, then check again.
5. Test with real questions before other people rely on it.

## Your three examples

- **Expense Policy Helper:** Role, Files and Memory. No routine.
- **AP Invoice Assistant:** adds Skills, read-only Connections and a daily Routine.
- **Month-End Close Tracker:** a Routine plus Memory of who owns what.

Keep your worksheets. The next time a colleague says "I spend every Monday doing...", you have a way to turn that into an agent.
